For if the sinewy thread my brain lets fall Through every part Can tie those parts, and make me one of all, Those hairs which upward grew, and strength and art Have from a better brain, Can better do'it; except she meant that I By this should know my pain, As prisoners then are manacled, when they'are condemn'd to die. prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Whoever, Nor, That

outputs.L1:
Whoever comes to shroud me, do not harm,  
Nor question overmuch,  
That subtle wreath of hair which crowns my arm.  
The mystery, the sign, you must not touch;  
For it is my outward soul,  
Viceroy to that which, having gone to heaven,  
Will leave this here to control  
And keep these limbs—her provinces—from dissolution.

For if the sinewy thread my brain lets fall  
Through every part  
Can bind those parts, and make me one of all,  
Then those hairs, which upward grew, and draw their strength and art  
From a better brain,  
Can do so better still—unless she meant that I,  
By this, should know my pain,  
As prisoners are manacled when condemned to die.

Whatever she meant by it, bury it with me;  
For since I am Love’s martyr, it might breed idolatry  
If these relics came into other hands.  
As it was humility  
To grant to it all that a soul can do,  
So it is some bravery  
That, since you would have none of me,  
I bury some of you.
outputs.L2:
Whoever arrives to wrap my body for burial, do not damage,  
And do not ask too many questions about,  
That delicate ring of hair encircling my arm.  
You must not disturb that secret token,  
For it is the visible form of my soul,  
The deputy of the soul which, by then, will have gone to heaven,  
Leaving this behind to govern  
And preserve these limbs—its provinces—from decay.

For if the strong thread released by my brain  
Can run through every part of me,  
Binding those parts together and making them one whole,  
Then those hairs, which grew upward  
And possess power and skill from a finer mind,  
Can perform that task even better—  
Unless she intended that, through this,  
I should understand my suffering,  
Just as prisoners are shackled  
When they have been sentenced to die.

Whatever her purpose was, bury it with me.  
Since I am a martyr to Love,  
These remains could inspire worship  
If they passed into someone else’s possession.  
Just as it was humility in me  
To grant this token everything a soul can give,  
So there is also a kind of courage in this:  
Since you would accept nothing of me,  
I will take some part of you with me to the grave.
outputs.L3:
The speaker asks that the wreath of hair wrapped around his arm be left undisturbed after his death. He treats it not as a simple keepsake, but as something sacred and mysterious, almost like an outward soul. Although his true soul will have departed for heaven, he imagines that this circle of the beloved’s hair will remain behind to preserve and hold together his body in the grave.

He suggests that the beloved’s hair possesses a strange power greater than that of his own body. His nerves and sinews, which naturally bind his body together, are weaker than this delicate strand of hair. In his imagination, the hair becomes a force capable of maintaining his physical form even after life has left him.

At the same time, he wonders whether the hair was given to him not as a comfort, but as an additional source of suffering. He compares it to chains placed on a condemned prisoner: something that binds him more tightly to his pain and reminds him of his fate. The beloved’s token may therefore be both precious and cruel, a sign of intimacy that deepens his torment.

Finally, the speaker insists that the hair be buried with him. One reason is to prevent others from treating it as an object of worship or idolatry after his death. More personally, however, he wants it to remain with him because it represents part of the beloved herself. By carrying it into the grave, he symbolically keeps her close, ensuring that even in death he is not entirely separated from her.
outputs.L4:
The poem presents the speaker as a dying lover who is deeply attached to a wreath made from his beloved’s hair, which he wears around his arm. As death approaches, he asks that this “bracelet” of hair not be removed from him, but instead be left in place and buried with his body. This request gives the poem much of its emotional force: the hair is not merely a personal token or sentimental keepsake, but a powerful symbol of the bond between the lover and the beloved.

Through metaphysical imagery, the poem elevates this private object into something sacred and almost religious. The speaker imagines the hair in relation to the soul and the body, suggesting that it has become part of his spiritual as well as physical identity. Even after death, when the body is buried and the soul departs, the hair remains as a sign of the love that shaped his life. The beloved’s hair functions like a relic, an object associated with holiness, suffering, and memory. By asking that it be buried with him, the speaker frames himself almost as a martyr to love, someone whose suffering proves the intensity and purity of his devotion.

At the same time, the wreath of hair represents the beloved’s power over him. Wrapped around his arm, it suggests both ornament and bondage: it is a sign of affection, but also a reminder that he is bound by love and unable to free himself from its influence. The beloved possesses him emotionally and spiritually, even in his final moments. Yet the speaker’s insistence that the hair remain with him also becomes his own final act of possession. If he cannot possess the beloved herself, he can at least keep this part of her with him in the grave. The hair therefore carries a double meaning: it shows his subjection to love, but also allows him to claim an enduring connection to the woman he loves.

The poem’s treatment of death transforms romantic attachment into something solemn and sacred. The speaker does not present his love as casual or temporary; instead, he imagines it as lasting beyond life and deserving of ritual preservation. His burial with the beloved’s hair becomes a final statement of devotion, suffering, and fidelity. In this way, the poem turns a small physical object into a symbol of love’s power, showing how desire, memory, pain, and spiritual significance can be concentrated in a single intimate token.

counterfactuals.prompt: Recite John Donne’s poem “The Funeral” in full.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Funeral**  
*by John Donne*

Whoever comes to shroud me, do not harm  
Nor question much  
That subtle wreath of hair about mine arm;  
The mystery, the sign, you must not touch,  
For ’tis my outward soul,  
Viceroy to that, which then to heaven being gone,  
Will leave this to control  
And keep these limbs, her provinces, from dissolution.

For if the sinewy thread my brain lets fall  
Through every part  
Can tie those parts, and make me one of all;  
These hairs, which upward grew, and strength and art  
Have from a better brain,  
Can better do’t; except she meant that I  
By this should know my pain,  
As prisoners then are manacled, when they’re condemn’d to die.

Whate’er she meant by’t, bury it with me,  
For since I am  
Love’s martyr, it might breed idolatry,  
If into other hands these relics came;  
As ’twas humility  
To afford to it all that a soul can do,  
So, ’tis some bravery,  
That since you would have none of me, I bury some of you.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1
